article_title: Proportional relationships decluttered—at last!
citation: James Tanton, Ted Coe, April Ström, Kyle Pearce. (2022). Proportional relationships decluttered—at last! White paper. https://www.nwea.org
title: Teach proportionality by focusing on ways of thinking rather than ways of doing
description: The paper's closing recommendation is that proportionality instruction should begin with the way of thinking of scaling in tandem rather than with standard procedures. It states: 'it makes perfect sense when we begin by focusing on ways of thinking (scaling in tandem), rather than ways of doing,' noting that throughout the article it never needed to 'set up a proportion or cross multiply.'
requirements: Instruction must present covarying measurable quantities and scaling reasoning before or instead of procedural shortcuts
constraints: The paper acknowledges 'There is much more to learn and discuss,' including connections to multiplication and division development and debates about definitions of ratios and rates
target_learners: middle grades and secondary mathematics students
target_learning_goals: develop robust conceptual understanding of proportionality
examples: Throughout the paper every problem, from exchange rates to the cats-and-rats teaser, is solved by scaling quantities directly rather than by cross multiplication
key_sources: Lb0

article_title: Exponential Change Brings Exponential Choice: Navigating Life, Learning, and Career
citation: Luna, C., & Weisgrau, J. (2025, March). Exponential Change Brings Exponential Choice: Navigating Life, Learning, and Career. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/244
title: Wayfinding: navigating non-linear life and career pathways through adaptability, agency, and transferable-skill recognition
description: The report frames envisioning the unfolding of one's life as an act of wayfinding, in which learners make effective decisions in complex situations and remain open to continuous learning. It argues the linear diploma-then-career journey is 'being replaced by a non-linear, ever-evolving path where adaptability, personal agency, and recognition of transferable skills are key to long-term success'. Schools are urged to help learners develop and practice these wayfinding skills through transitions.
requirements: Education institutions must prioritize helping learners develop and practice wayfinding skills through repeated transitions
constraints: The report presents wayfinding as an argumentative framework with personal anecdotes, not as a tested model
target_learners: youth transitioning to postsecondary and workforce pathways
target_learning_goals: adaptability
personal agency
navigation of life and career transitions
examples: Author anecdote of a childhood navigation game that the author credits with developing the mindsets enabling confident wayfinding through life changes
key_sources: Luna, C., & Weisgrau, J. (2025, March). Exponential Change Brings Exponential Choice: Navigating Life, Learning, and Career. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/244

article_title: Using Data to Improve School Climate: Insights from Three California Schools
citation: Klevan, S., Leung-Gagné, M., & Nakajima, T. M. (2024). Using data to improve school climate: Insights from three California schools. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/918.411
title: Four-domain framework of positive school climate (Safety, Community, Academics, Institutional Environment)
description: The report adopts a multidimensional conception of school climate organized into four domains drawn from Wang and Degol's review: "In a review of the literature on school climate, Wang and Degol (2016) outline 13 dimensions of school climate, which fall under four domains." Safety covers physical and emotional security and fair discipline; Community covers relationships, connectedness, and respect for diversity; Academics covers leadership, teaching and learning, and professional development; Institutional Environment covers structural features. The three case study schools focused mainly on the Safety and Community domains.
requirements: Understanding the dimensions of school climate is described as important for policymakers and practitioners to plan interventions that target student outcomes as intended
constraints: The case study schools were not focused on the institutional environment domain because features like class size and building quality are not typically under site-level leaders' control
target_learning_goals: improving school climate to support student well-being, engagement, and learning
examples: The report's Table 1 defines the three domains and their dimensions, adapted from Wang and Degol (2016), and the report's findings are organized by these domains and dimensions
key_sources: Klevan, S., Leung-Gagné, M., & Nakajima, T. M. (2024). Using data to improve school climate: Insights from three California schools. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/918.411

article_title: Using AI in engineering education: a balancing act, driven by clear purpose
citation: Kudina, O. (2025). Using AI in engineering education: a balancing act, driven by clear purpose. Draft version, to appear in The Routledge Handbook of the Philosophy of Engineering, 2nd ed.
title: Waterproof: an educational AI tool combining rule-based AI with a GenAI chat interface for writing mathematical proofs
description: Waterproof is an educational AI tool developed, tested and validated by Portegies et al. (2025) to help students develop mathematical proof-writing skills. It "combines more traditional rule-based AI" providing a library of proof examples with a GenAI chat-based interface that helps with students' challenges interactively. The combination mitigates the risk of misinformation (GenAI hallucinations) and induces students to develop proofs themselves while reflecting on the process.
requirements: Combination of rule-based and generative components to mitigate hallucination risk
constraints: Described in the mathematics field; the chapter presents it as an example of augmented AI use accompanying teacher-led learning
target_learning_goals: writing mathematical proofs
metacognitive reflection on proof development
examples: Students develop their own proofs in a declarative manner, explaining the results and logic, with chat-based GenAI support
key_sources: Kudina, O. (2025). Using AI in engineering education: a balancing act, driven by clear purpose. Draft version, to appear in The Routledge Handbook of the Philosophy of Engineering, 2nd ed. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.16626

article_title: Generative AI as a Design Variable: An Evidence-Centered Framework for Principled Governance in STEM Assessment
citation: Gao, Y., Chen, Z., Li, M., & Zhai, X. (2026). Generative AI as a Design Variable: An Evidence-Centered Framework for Principled Governance in STEM Assessment.
title: Water Balloon Physics Image Require-GenAI task
description: A second Require-GenAI task in which GenAI has a dual role: "it is simultaneously the source of the artifact being analyzed and the tool students use to correct it." Students receive a GenAI-generated image of a child swinging a water balloon in horizontal circles, identify physically impossible elements, use GenAI to generate a more accurate image, and ask GenAI to construct a correct free body diagram. A three-way error classification (what GenAI identified, what the student identified independently, what the student believes GenAI misidentified) makes independent judgment directly observable and separable from AI contribution.
requirements: The accuracy-ceiling criterion: GenAI consistently missed at least one expert-anchored error in the image and FBD, as confirmed by the expert answer key
constraints: A student who cannot independently identify errors beyond what GenAI flags produces an artifact that fails the distinguishability condition
target_learning_goals: Independent identification of Newtonian mechanics violations and physics-grounded critique of AI-generated diagrams
examples: The expert answer key identifies string angle, balloon deformation, and spurious centripetal force addition as key errors
key_sources: Gao, Y., Chen, Z., Li, M., & Zhai, X. (2026). Generative AI as a Design Variable: An Evidence-Centered Framework for Principled Governance in STEM Assessment. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.24837

article_title: Students' Epistemological Beliefs and their Chatbot Preferences in AI-mediated Physics Learning
citation: Amogh Sirnoorkar and Omkar Mamidpalliwar. (2026). Students' Epistemological Beliefs and their Chatbot Preferences in AI-mediated Physics Learning. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.29385
title: Custom-built online waves module with simulations integrated with a chatbot
description: A 10-page extra-credit online activity on wave concepts, built for a large-enrollment calculus-based physics course for future engineers using the Matter and Interactions textbook. Each content page presented "an interactive simulation and followed by four questions", with a chatbot integrated throughout. The first page collected anticipated chatbot preferences among three options, and the last page collected student ID, a 5-point activity rating, perceived learning, qualitative feedback, and retrospective reflections on content familiarity and chatbot preferences. Estimated completion time was around 30-45 minutes.
requirements: Administered as an extra-credit activity with students informed it was not part of course assessment, to encourage honest participation
constraints: The module covered waves because the topic was not covered in the host course
target_learners: introductory calculus-based physics students for future engineers
target_learning_goals: wave concepts not covered in the host course
examples: Deployed in Spring of 2026 in a course with total enrollment around 1800; 1191 students responded to the activity
key_sources: Amogh Sirnoorkar and Omkar Mamidpalliwar. (2026). Students' Epistemological Beliefs and their Chatbot Preferences in AI-mediated Physics Learning. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.29385

article_title: Knowing Its Name, Not Its Nature: Word Association Mapping of Student AI Cognition and Evidence-Based Micro-Credential Design in Turkish Higher Education
citation: İsmail Şan and Hanife Gülhan Orhan Karsak. (2026). Knowing its name, not its nature: word association mapping of student AI cognition and evidence-based micro-credential design in Turkish higher education. International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s41239-026-00621-w
title: Word Association Test as a cognitive-structure diagnostic instrument for needs-assessment-driven curriculum design
description: The Word Association Test (WAT) is a psycholinguistic instrument grounded in spreading-activation and associationist models of semantic memory, used here to map the organisational structure of students' AI cognition. The article explains that the test "measures cognitive structure not as the presence or absence of individual concepts but as the pattern of associative connections among them". Early, frequent responses indicate highly integrated concepts; late or rare responses indicate peripheral or fragmented understanding. The study operationalises this through a seven-stage protocol — normalisation to 65 canonical codes, frequency and Z-score banding, Kendall's τ with FDR correction, PROXSCAL multidimensional scaling, and hierarchical threshold network analysis — and links the resulting map directly to micro-credential design decisions.
requirements: Administration with a time limit and no prompting to promote spontaneous activation, as the study implemented with a three-minute limit
constraints: The article notes semantic distance reveals the existence of a relationship rather than its specific nature

The sample excludes Turkey's most research-intensive and technologically advanced universities, so the authors advise against generalising to institutions of that profile without independent empirical verification
target_learning_goals: mapping learners' existing cognitive structures around AI to inform AI literacy curriculum sequencing
examples: The study administered an online written WAT with the stimulus word 'artificial intelligence' to 436 students at four Turkish public universities, yielding 1376 raw tokens analysed through the seven-stage protocol
key_sources: İsmail Şan and Hanife Gülhan Orhan Karsak. (2026). Knowing its name, not its nature: word association mapping of student AI cognition and evidence-based micro-credential design in Turkish higher education. International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s41239-026-00621-w

article_title: Guidance in computer-supported collaborative inquiry learning: Capturing aspects of affect and teacher support in science classrooms
citation: Tarja Pietarinen · Tuire Palonen · Marja Vauras. (2021). Guidance in computer-supported collaborative inquiry learning: Capturing aspects of affect and teacher support in science classrooms. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn, 16, 261–287. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-021-09347-5
title: Shared orchestration pattern: whole-class introduction, walking around, group observation and occasional whole-class announcements
description: During technology-enhanced collaborative inquiry without dedicated orchestration tools, all four teachers followed a common classroom orchestration pattern. As the article describes it, they "started with a joint introduction, then walked around the classroom, observing and assessing group performance and occasionally making whole-class announcements, which is in line with the empirical findings of Greiffenhagen (2012)". When walking around, teachers regularly stopped by a group, provided help if needed, and followed the group activity until the target problem was solved before moving on, so groups were not left prematurely without guidance.
requirements: A teacher present in the classroom circulating among autonomous small groups
A technological environment students can largely operate without constant intervention
constraints: Teachers in the study were novices at guiding students in the VLE; time spent observing (over a third of attention) may partly reflect unfamiliarity with the environment
target_learners: High school science students working in small groups
target_learning_goals: Sustaining collaborative scientific inquiry in a virtual laboratory
examples: All four teachers observed their groups and provided task- and technical-related guidance, while socio-emotional support and off-topic discussions occurred only with some groups
key_sources: Tarja Pietarinen · Tuire Palonen · Marja Vauras. (2021). Guidance in computer-supported collaborative inquiry learning: Capturing aspects of affect and teacher support in science classrooms. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn, 16, 261–287. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-021-09347-5

article_title: Walking the number line: towards an enactive understanding of integer arithmetic
citation: Jacqueline Anton, Dor Abrahamson. (2025). Walking the number line: towards an enactive understanding of integer arithmetic. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09707-w
title: Walking number line design: body-scale number line plus desk-scale number line with figurine, using a four-step orientation-and-movement procedure
description: The design consists of a body-scale number line (a 20' × 4' paper roll displaying a number line from −5 to +5, with step-spaced marks and addition/subtraction signs at the ends) and a small number line (an 8.5″ × 11″ sheet with a scaled-down line and a puppy figurine). Students follow four steps: "start by standing on the first number in the problem"; face the addition or subtraction direction; "walk forwards if the second number (the addend or subtrahend) is positive and backwards if the second number is negative"; and walk as many steps as the absolute value of that second number. The operation is enacted as a shift in orientation and the second number's polarity as direction of movement.
requirements: Signs marking addition and subtraction at the two ends of the body-scale line
A figurine on the desk-scale line for re-enacting the walking solution
constraints: The material boundaries at −5 and +5 led some students to reject solutions outside that range, per the limitations section
target_learners: Grade 7 students in general education inclusive math classes, pre-identified as struggling with integer operations
target_learning_goals: fluency with adding and subtracting positive and negative integers
examples: A student solving −1 + 3 stands on −1, faces addition, and walks forwards three steps to arrive at 2
key_sources: Jacqueline Anton, Dor Abrahamson. (2025). Walking the number line: towards an enactive understanding of integer arithmetic. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09707-w

article_title: Supplemental Material for Spontaneous Use of Retrieval and Rereading: Relation to Achievement Goals and Exam Performance
citation: Aleza Wallace, Andrew J. Elliot, & Ronald Rogge. Spontaneous Use of Retrieval and Rereading: Relation to Achievement Goals and Exam Performance. https://osf.io/53z6x
title: Open Science Framework repository (osf.io/53z6x) with the study's data and materials
description: A public, open-access OSF repository associated with the study on spontaneous use of retrieval and rereading. The disclosure form lists it for both the Open Data Badge and the Open Materials Badge, stating it provides "the URL , doi , or other permanent path for accessing the time-stamped and immutable data in a public, open-access repository". The authors confirm "sufficient information for an independent researcher to reproduce all of the reported results" and the methodology. No year of posting is printed in the supplied text.
requirements: A qualifying public, open-access repository that keeps the shared information accessible via the web in perpetuity, with the information in a format that is time-stamped, immutable, and permanent, as the form requires for badge eligibility
constraints: The form notes there are circumstances in which sharing participants' data could violate confidentiality, and publicly posted data must not contain information that would allow individuals to be identified without consent
target_learners: college students in the underlying exam-performance study
target_learning_goals: self-regulated study behavior, specifically spontaneous use of retrieval and rereading
examples: The authors checked the Open Data and Open Materials badges and supplied osf.io/53z6x as the permanent path for both the data and the materials

article_title: A Novel Approach to Reading.
citation: L. Z. (1922). A Novel Approach to Reading. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://eric.ed.gov/?q=journal+of+educational+psychology
title: A silent reading method for beginners built on printed commands executed as action responses
description: Watkins' Silent Reading Method teaches beginners to read by having each pupil carry out printed commands physically in front of the class. The commands mix parts of speech and varied actions, e.g. pupils must 'Draw an oblong, a circle and a square' or ask a visitor a question and report the answer. The materials were made 'available so that anyone may attempt to do what she has found possible by actual trial.'
requirements: available printed materials so that anyone may attempt the method
class activities involving other people, objects and actions in the room
constraints: the reviewer notes it is not supposed to displace instruction in literary appreciation and extensive reading
target_learners: beginning readers in the first school year
target_learning_goals: silent reading comprehension of printed commands
examples: pupils in a class of forty carried out printed commands such as telling a visitor a fact and showing a time on a large dial
key_sources: L. Z. (1922). A Novel Approach to Reading. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://eric.ed.gov/?q=journal+of+educational+psychology

article_title: The new clinical psychology and the psycho-clinicist. Part II. The psychological clinic and the public schools.
citation: J. K. W. Wallin. (1911). The New Clinical Psychology and the Psycho-Clinicist. Part II. The Psychological Clinic and the Public Schools. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://psycnet.apa.org/journal/edu
title: Bureau of school research as a central clearing-house for educational data
description: A proposed central school department in charge of a director who is an expert in child, educational and clinical psychology with experimental pedagogy and teaching experience. The article argues investigation results are liable to run to sand unless they are "properly unified, correlated and brought to a focus", and that the bureau should gather, compile, compare, correlate, interpret and turn to practical use data from five sources: medico-dental examination records, sociological case data, pedagogical records, controlled educational experiments, and psycho-clinical records.
requirements: A director who is an expert in child, educational and clinical psychology, familiar with experimental pedagogy, with practical teaching experience and some knowledge of medical inspection work
constraints: The author frames the plan as aspirational for school systems; he notes that where a comprehensive bureau is not feasible, a clinical laboratory alone should claim first attention
target_learners: public-school pupils, particularly exceptional, retarded and delinquent children
target_learning_goals: scientific diagnosis and classification of pupils' health, development and pedagogical status
examples: The Chicago public schools' department of child study and pedagogic investigation, established in 1899, is cited as the one outstanding existing exception conducting studies and issuing annual reports
key_sources: J. K. W. Wallin. (1911). The New Clinical Psychology and the Psycho-Clinicist. Part II. The Psychological Clinic and the Public Schools. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://psycnet.apa.org/journal/edu

article_title: The new clinical psychology and the psycho-clinicist. Part II. The psychological clinic and the public schools.
citation: J. K. W. Wallin. (1911). The New Clinical Psychology and the Psycho-Clinicist. Part II. The Psychological Clinic and the Public Schools. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://psycnet.apa.org/journal/edu
title: Four ages of the child: chronological, physiological, pedagogical and psychical
description: Wallin's framework for analyzing retardation: a child's development can be indexed on four independent ages, so a single chronological age may mask divergent developmental status. He states that "a child has at least four ages: a chronological, a physiological, a pedagogical and a psychical," illustrating with a 15-year-old who may be physiologically, pedagogically and psychically younger. Mental age must be determined independently by serial graded age tests, since pedagogical retardation may reflect late entrance or undeserved promotion rather than mental defect.
requirements: Reliable normal norms and graded serial age tests to determine mental age independently of school progress
constraints: The framework presumes measurement instruments (such as the Binet-Simon scale) whose norms the article itself notes are not yet validated for American children
target_learners: school pupils, especially pedagogically retarded children
target_learning_goals: accurate diagnosis of the source and degree of a pupil's retardation
examples: The article's worked example of a 15-year-old who is physiologically 13, pedagogically 12, and psychically 11
key_sources: J. K. W. Wallin. (1911). The New Clinical Psychology and the Psycho-Clinicist. Part II. The Psychological Clinic and the Public Schools. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://psycnet.apa.org/journal/edu

article_title: The new clinical psychology and the psycho-clinicist. Part II. The psychological clinic and the public schools.
citation: J. K. W. Wallin. (1911). The New Clinical Psychology and the Psycho-Clinicist. Part II. The Psychological Clinic and the Public Schools. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://psycnet.apa.org/journal/edu
title: Five functions of the school psycho-clinical laboratory
description: The article specifies a five-part functional charter for a school clinical laboratory serving exceptional children: clinical examination of exceptional children, establishment of reliable norms for normal children, acting as a clearing-house for placing exceptional children in appropriate special schools or institutions, training teachers in psycho-clinical testing methods, and supervising special-school curricula while offering courses on the psychology of mental deficiency. Its central aim is "the scientific investigation of abnormalities of development", with examination including graded serial tests, form-board and sensory-motor tests, standardized intellectual tests, and anthropometric measures, and percentile curves plotted for each child.
requirements: Full data from the other sources (medical, sociological, pedagogical) so the laboratory can perform its clearing-house function, and reliable norms for typical normal children against which to plot percentile curves
constraints: The laboratory cannot examine all pupils needing examination in a large school system, so testing must be partly delegated to trained special-room teachers; recommendations of the director are not subject to reversal except by the board or superintendent
target_learners: exceptional children: pedagogically retarded, subnormal, supernormal and delinquent pupils
target_learning_goals: diagnosis, classification and placement of exceptional children, and establishment of developmental norms
examples: Children mentally retarded more than four years are classed as probably permanently arrested institutional cases and separated from the merely retarded or backward
key_sources: J. K. W. Wallin. (1911). The New Clinical Psychology and the Psycho-Clinicist. Part II. The Psychological Clinic and the Public Schools. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://psycnet.apa.org/journal/edu

article_title: Frontal midline theta transcranial alternating current stimulation enhances early consolidation of episodic memory
citation: Limor Shtoots, Asher Nadler, Roni Partouche, Dorin Sharir, Aryeh Rothstein, Liran Shati & Daniel A. Levy. (2024). Frontal midline theta transcranial alternating current stimulation enhances early consolidation of episodic memory. npj Science of Learning 9:8. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00222-0
title: Insert a washout period between post-learning stimulation and memory assessment to attribute benefits to consolidation rather than retrieval
description: When assessing whether a post-learning intervention benefits consolidation, the article recommends delaying the first memory test long enough for stimulation aftereffects to dissipate. The 2-h break "was implemented as a washout period in order to separate the effects of stimulation on early consolidation from the lingering effects of such stimulation on retrieval." The rationale draws on reports that alpha-band tACS aftereffects washed out once 70 min had passed, so testing at 120 min provided added caution.
requirements: Knowledge of how long stimulation aftereffects persist, so the washout duration exceeds the reported persistence window
constraints: The article notes reports of persistent theta increase following tACS are rarer than for alpha, so the 120-min delay is a precaution rather than a proven boundary
target_learning_goals: episodic memory for studied object pictures
examples: Participants were tested 120 min after stimulation ended, by which time theta stimulation aftereffects would arguably have washed out, so benefits could be attributed to consolidation
key_sources: Limor Shtoots, Asher Nadler, Roni Partouche, Dorin Sharir, Aryeh Rothstein, Liran Shati & Daniel A. Levy. (2024). Frontal midline theta transcranial alternating current stimulation enhances early consolidation of episodic memory. npj Science of Learning 9:8. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00222-0

article_title: A Multimedia Adaptive Tutoring System for Mathematics that Addresses Cognition, Metacognition and Affect
citation: Arroyo, I., Woolf, B. P., Burelson, W., Muldner, K., Rai, D., & Tai, M. (2014). A Multimedia Adaptive Tutoring System for Mathematics that Addresses Cognition, Metacognition and Affect. Int J Artif Intell Educ 24:387–426. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-014-0023-y
title: Wayang Outpost / MathSpring multimedia mathematics tutoring system
description: Wayang Outpost, now called MathSpring, is a multimedia-based intelligent tutoring system for mathematics built on cognitive apprenticeship theory. It models solutions "via worked-out examples with the use of sound and animation, and provides practice opportunities on math word problems", mostly released MCAS and SAT items clustered into coarse-grained knowledge units so students must classify problem types. It provides multimedia hints implementing Mayer's principles, adaptive difficulty selection, animated affective learning companions, and teacher tools reporting progress per skill mapped to Common Core standards.
requirements: Content organized as clustered high-stakes test items within knowledge units
Log data from past students to estimate item difficulty and expected behavior
constraints: Knowledge units are more coarse-grained than most other math tutoring systems, with only pairs or triplets of problems highly similar and parameterized
There is no explicit scaffold-fading procedure; help fading happens naturally through transfer to similar-difficulty problems
target_learners: middle and high school students preparing for standardized mathematics tests
target_learning_goals: mathematics problem solving
problem-type identification and classification
test readiness
examples: Students preparing to retake the 10th grade MCAS test used Wayang in regular math classes before the statewide exam
key_sources: Arroyo, I., Woolf, B. P., Burelson, W., Muldner, K., Rai, D., & Tai, M. (2014). A Multimedia Adaptive Tutoring System for Mathematics that Addresses Cognition, Metacognition and Affect. Int J Artif Intell Educ 24:387–426. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-014-0023-y

article_title: Reasoning Mind Genie 2: An Intelligent Tutoring System as a Vehicle for International Transfer of Instructional Methods in Mathematics
citation: Khachatryan, G. A., Romashov, A. V., Khachatryan, A. R., Gaudino, S. J., Khachatryan, J. M., Guarian, K. R., & Yufa, N. V. (2014). Reasoning Mind Genie 2: An Intelligent Tutoring System as a Vehicle for International Transfer of Instructional Methods in Mathematics. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-014-0019-7
title: Wall of Mastery: a mastery-based mode for advancing through difficulty levels on covered objectives
description: Wall of Mastery is a Genie 2 mode added "as a systematic way for students to learn to solve level B and C problems on each objective presented in Guided Study". After an objective is covered, the level A cell in its row becomes enabled; completing a cell's problem sequence with high accuracy marks it complete and enables the next difficulty cell. The article describes it as "a rudimentary open learner model", noting learner control is likely more appropriate for advanced problem solving over previously studied topics than for basic instruction.
requirements: The corresponding objective must first be covered in Guided Study
Students must complete problems with high accuracy to unlock the next difficulty level
constraints: Positioned for advanced problems over previously studied topics rather than first-time instruction
target_learners: Grades 2–6 students using Genie 2 who have completed objectives in Guided Study
target_learning_goals: Mastery of more advanced (level B and C) problems on previously studied objectives

Reasoning Mind Genie 2: An Intelligent Tutoring System as a Vehicle for International Transfer of Instructional Methods in Mathematics. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-014-0019-7

article_title: Preface-Emerging Technologies and Landmark Systems for Learning Mathematics and Science: Dedicated to the Memory of Erica Melis-Part 2
citation: Sergey Sosnovsky & Bruce M. McLaren & Vincent Aleven. (2014). Preface-Emerging Technologies and Landmark Systems for Learning Mathematics and Science: Dedicated to the Memory of Erica Melis-Part 2. Int J Artif Intell Educ 24. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-014-0025-9
title: Wayang Outpost (MathSpring): intelligent tutoring system for middle-school mathematics combining cognitive apprenticeship, multimedia learning and multidimensional personalization
description: Wayang Outpost, later MathSpring, is an intelligent tutoring system for middle-school mathematics described in this special issue. It "combines principles of cognitive apprenticeship and multimedia learning to implement a range of coaching and scaffolding approaches helping students develop problem-solving skills." It adapts in both the outer loop (problem selection, informing students of their learning state) and the inner loop (instructional videos, elaborate feedback, step-by-step worked-out examples of similar problems). The system has been used in mathematics classrooms since 2003 and the accompanying paper presents extensive empirical evidence for its effectiveness.
requirements: Tracking of learner cognitive, metacognitive and affective states to drive adaptive pedagogical decisions
target_learning_goals: mathematical problem-solving skills
examples: Used in mathematics classrooms since 2003; outer-loop adaptation selects problems of appropriate difficulty and inner-loop adaptation provides videos, elaborate feedback and worked-out examples.
key_sources: Sergey Sosnovsky & Bruce M. McLaren & Vincent Aleven. (2014). Preface-Emerging Technologies and Landmark Systems for Learning Mathematics and Science: Dedicated to the Memory of Erica Melis-Part 2. Int J Artif Intell Educ 24. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-014-0025-9

article_title: The Impact of Looking Further Ahead: A Comparison of Two Data-driven Unsolicited Hint Types on Performance in an Intelligent Data-driven Logic Tutor
citation: Christa Cody, Mehak Maniktala, Nicholas Lytle, Min Chi, Tiffany Barnes. (2021). The Impact of Looking Further Ahead: A Comparison of Two Data-driven Unsolicited Hint Types on Performance in an Intelligent Data-driven Logic Tutor. https://arxiv.org/abs/2102.05741
title: Waypoint hints: data-driven subgoal hints 2-3 steps ahead
description: Waypoints are a new hint type created by modifying the Next-Step hint generator to select target statements 2-3 steps away from the student's current state, among which the state with higher frequency within prior correct solutions is chosen. They are intended to serve as near-term subgoals, giving students more room to explore the solution space and develop their own problem-solving strategies without expert labelling. Expert review of a random sample verified this simple algorithm produces hints similar to those from data-driven Approach Maps.
requirements: A Hint Factory-style interaction network built from historical correct student solutions
constraints: Waypoints take longer to justify and resulted in fewer hints by design; the authors note more scaffolding may be needed to help students follow them
target_learners: undergraduate students learning formal logic proofs
target_learning_goals: problem-solving subgoal identification and multi-step proof planning
examples: In the Deep Thought study, Waypoint hints appeared as unsolicited Assertions during training problems, capped at 1/3 of the problem length
key_sources: Christa Cody, Mehak Maniktala, Nicholas Lytle, Min Chi, Tiffany Barnes. (2021). The Impact of Looking Further Ahead: A Comparison of Two Data-driven Unsolicited Hint Types on Performance in an Intelligent Data-driven Logic Tutor. https://arxiv.org/abs/2102.05741

article_title: Preface: Reflections on the waves of emerging learning technologies
citation: Curtis J. Bonk, David A. Wiley. (2020). Preface: Reflections on the waves of emerging learning technologies. Education Tech Research Dev 68:1595–1612. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09809-x
title: Waves taxonomy of emerging learning technologies: extended, connected, and repeated waves
description: The article organizes decades of emerging learning technologies into a three-part taxonomy of waves. Some waves persist over long periods (extended), some link to earlier or later technologies (connected), and some recur cyclically as they go in and out of favor (repeated). The authors state that "some waves are extended over time whereas some are connected to other waves and still others are repeated in cycles as they go in and out of favor," and use this framework to structure their historical account of collaborative writing tools, videoconferencing, blended learning, and open content.
requirements: A historical perspective spanning multiple decades of technology adoption in education
constraints: The taxonomy is a reflective organizing lens offered by the authors, not an empirically tested classification
target_learning_goals: understanding the historical evolution of learning technologies
examples: Collaborative writing tools as an extended wave; synchronous videoconferencing as a connected wave; blended learning and open content as repeated waves
key_sources: Curtis J. Bonk, David A. Wiley. (2020). Preface: Reflections on the waves of emerging learning technologies. Education Tech Research Dev 68:1595–1612. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09809-x

article_title: Co-designing a pedagogical framework and principles for a hybrid STEM learning environment design
citation: Mäkelä, T., Fenyvesi, K., Kankaanranta, M., Pnevmatikos, D., & Christodoulou, P. (2022). Co-designing a pedagogical framework and principles for a hybrid STEM learning environment. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-022-10114-y
title: Ways of teaching and learning: eleven design principles for STEM environments
description: This framework category contains eleven principles covering active knowledge construction, participation and involvement, collaborative learning, learning through experiences, experiments and inquiry, project-based STEM learning, self-regulated learning, reflective learning, ICT-enhanced learning, games and gamification, and multiple representations. The article reports that "A total of 11 design principles related to ways of teaching and learning (Table 5) emerged as a result of focus group 1 discussions and were confirmed as important in focus group 2". Each principle carries supporting literature and a concrete example.
requirements: Principles confirmed in focus group 2 and verified or modified in focus group 3
target_learning_goals: active knowledge construction
collaboration
inquiry
self-regulation
reflection
ICT and game-enhanced learning
examples: Principle 3.5 Experiments and inquiry is exemplified by modelling processes of scientific inquiry in virtual or physical laboratories

article_title: Analysis of Nurses' and Physicians' Attitudes, Knowledge, and Perceptions toward Fever in Children: A Systematic Review with Meta-Analysis.
citation: Vicens-Blanes, F., Miró-Bonet, R., & Molina-Mula, J. (2021). Analysis of Nurses' and Physicians' Attitudes, Knowledge, and Perceptions toward Fever in Children: A Systematic Review with Meta-Analysis. International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health. https://doi.org/10.3390/ijerph182312444
title: Walsh et al. fever management survey (FMK, FMA, FMP)
description: A structured self-administered questionnaire developed by Walsh et al. in 2005, divided into three questionnaires: "fever management knowledge (FMK), fever management attitudes (FMA), and fever management practices (FMP)". It was the dominant measurement instrument in the educational-program studies the review analyzed: four of the programs applied or adapted it, while one study used a validated questionnaire created by its authors and another used an unvalidated questionnaire to evaluate knowledge.
requirements: Administered as a structured self-administered questionnaire in pre-test and post-test evaluations of educational programs.
constraints: The review notes the use of unvalidated questionnaires in some articles may restrict the validity of results; one included study used an unvalidated questionnaire to evaluate knowledge.
target_learning_goals: measuring fever management knowledge
measuring fever management attitudes
measuring fever management practices
examples: Four of the educational-program studies included in the meta-analysis applied or adapted the Walsh et al. 2005 survey.

Analysis of Nurses' and Physicians' Attitudes, Knowledge, and Perceptions toward Fever in Children: A Systematic Review with Meta-Analysis. article_title: Exploration of the Factors That Support Learning: Web-Based Activity and Testing Systems in Community College Algebra [Contributed Report]
citation: Shandy Hauk, Bryan Matlen, Larry Thomas. (2017). Exploration of the Factors that Support Learning: Web-based Activity and Testing Systems in Community College Algebra. 20th Annual Conference on Research in Undergraduate Mathematics Education. https://sigmaa.maa.org/rume
title: Two-dimensional framework classifying digital learning environments by adaptivity and basis in an explicit model of learning
description: The article frames web-based learning environments along two dimensions: "the extent to which they adaptively respond to student behavior and (2) the extent to which they are based on a careful cognitive model". Static environments deliver fixed-order content with identical feedback; dynamic environments track behavior (errors, error rates, time-on-problem) and use a programmed decision tree to select problem sets and feedback based on estimated skill mastery; cognitively-based dynamic systems additionally encode the cognitive processing needed for skill acquisition and can adapt and fade scaffolds. Examples named include ALEKS, Khan Academy, ActiveMath, and Cognitive Tutor.
requirements: Distinguishing environment types requires specifying whether student behavior is tracked and whether an explicit theory of learning drives design and implementation
constraints: The article notes no fully tested cognitively-based system currently exists for college students learning algebra
target_learners: community college students in elementary algebra
target_learning_goals: algebraic knowledge and skills
examples: Khan Academy's mastery challenge: once a student gets six items in a row correct, the next level of items in a programmed target learning trajectory is offered, with the analyzer assembling the next set based on error type.
key_sources: Shandy Hauk, Bryan Matlen, Larry Thomas. (2017). Exploration of the Factors that Support Learning: Web-based Activity and Testing Systems in Community College Algebra. 20th Annual Conference on Research in Undergraduate Mathematics Education. https://sigmaa.maa.org/rume

article_title: Exploration of the Factors That Support Learning: Web-Based Activity and Testing Systems in Community College Algebra [Contributed Report]
citation: Shandy Hauk, Bryan Matlen, Larry Thomas. (2017). Exploration of the Factors that Support Learning: Web-based Activity and Testing Systems in Community College Algebra. 20th Annual Conference on Research in Undergraduate Mathematics Education. https://sigmaa.maa.org/rume
title: WATS platform: adaptive problem sets, instructional videos, and data-driven instructor monitoring tools used as replacement for seatwork and homework
description: The investigated WATS is accessed on the internet and "designed primarily for use as replacement for some in-class individual seatwork and some homework". Like the study's system, some WATS tools "include adaptive problem sets, instructional videos, and data-driven tools for instructors to use to monitor and scaffold student learning". The platform's resources include practice items, "mastery mechanics," analytics, and coaching tools, per the fidelity rubric's educative component.
requirements: Instructors participate for two semesters, with a fall field-test semester before the spring efficacy semester, to familiarize themselves with implementing the WATS with their local algebra curriculum
constraints: Developers paid attention to learning theory for system content, but implementation processes and structures were under-specified; the instructor role in mediating learning was not clearly defined
target_learners: community college students in elementary algebra
target_learning_goals: algebraic knowledge, skill practice, and mastery
examples: In the cluster randomized trial, half of instructors at each site were assigned to use the WATS (treatment) while the other half taught as usual without it (control).
key_sources: Shandy Hauk, Bryan Matlen, Larry Thomas. (2017). Exploration of the Factors that Support Learning: Web-based Activity and Testing Systems in Community College Algebra. 20th Annual Conference on Research in Undergraduate Mathematics Education. https://sigmaa.maa.org/rume

article_title: The Effect of Using Cartoons on Developing Omani Grade 4 Students' Awareness of Water Issues and Their Attitudes towards Using Them in Teaching Social Studies
citation: Al-Rabaani, A. H., & Al-AAmri, I. H. (2017). The Effect of Using Cartoons on Developing Omani Grade 4 Students’ Awareness of Water Issues and their Attitudes towards Using them in Teaching Social Studies. Journal of Social Studies Education Research, 8(1), 35-46. https://www.jsser.org
title: Water-awareness test and cartoon-attitudes questionnaire instruments
description: The study used two researcher-developed instruments. The awareness test was built from analysis of the Grade 4 Social Studies textbook water unit and "consisted of 20 questions" including multiple choice, completion and open items. The attitudes questionnaire used a five-point Likert scale with 13 items in two domains. Validity was checked by a panel of judges from Sultan Qaboos University and Ministry of Education supervisors; reliabilities were .74 and .89.
requirements: Validity examined by a panel of judges from Sultan Qaboos University and social studies supervisors from the Ministry of Education
constraints: Reliability of the awareness test (.74) was established on a trial group of 30 students from different schools; the questionnaire reliability (.89) was obtained only from the experimental group after treatment
target_learning_goals: Awareness of water issues
Attitudes toward cartoons as a teaching tool
examples: The pretest and questionnaire were administered on 5 April; implementation ran three weeks, three lessons per week, from 12 April 2015 till 30 April 2015.

The Effect of Using Cartoons on Developing Omani Grade 4 Students’ Awareness of Water Issues and their Attitudes towards Using them in Teaching Social Studies. Journal of Social Studies Education Research, 8(1), 35-46. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1141986

article_title: Effect of Educational Games on Social Skills in Iranian Mentally Retarded Children
citation: Shakibaei, Z., Rahimaghaee, F., & Arish, M. (2013). Effect of Educational Games on Social Skills in Iranian Mentally Retarded Children. li-manager's Journal of Educational Psychology, 6(4).
title: Wailand's social growth scale as the outcome measure
description: Wailand's social growth scale is the instrument used to measure social maturity in this study. It "covers birth to older than 25 years" with age-specific questions to age 12 and common questions thereafter; it "has 117 items but 84 items were questioned" for these children aged 12 and younger. Items fall in eight categories including self-help general, eating, dressing, direction, occupation, communication, locomotion and socialization, and answers are rated 0, 0.5 and 1 to compute a social quotient.
requirements: Respondents must be able to take part in sessions and, in this sample, be able to speak and not be deaf
constraints: The article states common questions must be answered for ages above 12, so the full item set was not used for this young sample
target_learning_goals: daily-life social and self-help abilities measured as social maturity
examples: Used as pre-test and post-test in both test and control groups; reliability was reported by the article as Cronbach's alpha (0.086)
key_sources: Shakibaei, Z., Rahimaghaee, F., & Arish, M. (2013). Effect of Educational Games on Social Skills in Iranian Mentally Retarded Children. li-manager's Journal of Educational Psychology, 6(4). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1101771

article_title: Evaluating the Effectiveness of Tools for Online Database Instruction
citation: Mery, Y., DeFrain, E., Kline, E., & Sult, L. (2014). Evaluating the Effectiveness of Tools for Online Database Instruction. Communications in Information Literacy, 8(1). https://journals.lib.pdx.edu/index.php/informationliteracy
title: WASSAIL open-source test delivery database and 16-item post-test instrument
description: Researchers created 16 multiple-choice test items based on the tutorials' learning outcomes, reviewed by librarians for content validity, each with four options plus an "I don't know" option. The items were loaded into WASSAIL, described in the article as "an open source web -based database from the University of Alberta Libraries that allows for the creation, management, and delivery of test items." The instrument served as the sole outcome measure for all three groups.
requirements: Content validity was established by showing items to several librarians and revising them per feedback.
constraints: The authors state the post-test was intentionally brief, that some items were poor (control outperformed both treatment groups on item 5), and that no reliability tests of the items could be conducted.
target_learning_goals: database searching skills
information literacy
examples: All 90 participants completed the identical 16-item post-test delivered through WASSAIL after their assigned condition.
key_sources: Mery, Y., DeFrain, E., Kline, E., & Sult, L. (2014). Evaluating the Effectiveness of Tools for Online Database Instruction. Communications in Information Literacy, 8(1). https://journals.lib.pdx.edu/index.php/informationliteracy

article_title: The Effect of Mock Tests on Iranian EFL Learners' Test Scores
citation: Hossein Khodabakhshzadeh, Reza Zardkanloo, Iman Alipoor. (2017). The Effect of Mock Tests on Iranian EFL learners’ Test Scores. International Journal of Education & Literacy Studies 5(3). http://dx.doi.org/10.7575/aiac.ijels.v.5n.3p.47
title: Washback effect: test preparation can produce both negative and positive washback depending on context
description: Washback is the influence of tests on teaching and learning. The article presents it as a contested, two-sided phenomenon: negative washback focuses learners' attention solely on the test so "they learn language for the sake of good score," while positive washback "prepares the learners for the test and eventually brings about good results for them." Citing Alderson and Wall (1993), the article holds that washback is "a context-bound issue" and that understanding of it is not usually supported by empirical evidence, motivating this study of mock tests in the Iranian IELTS context.
requirements: Empirical research in specific contexts, since washback claims are context-bound
constraints: The article states washback understanding "is not usually supported by empirical evidence" and more research is required
target_learners: Language learners in high-stakes test preparation courses
target_learning_goals: Performance on high-stakes language tests such as IELTS and TOEFL
examples: The study tested one washback question in one context: whether mock IELTS tests positively affect Iranian candidates' overall IELTS scores
key_sources: Hossein Khodabakhshzadeh, Reza Zardkanloo, Iman Alipoor. (2017). The Effect of Mock Tests on Iranian EFL learners’ Test Scores. International Journal of Education & Literacy Studies 5(3). http://dx.doi.org/10.7575/aiac.ijels.v.5n.3p.47

article_title: The Effect of TMPT Program on Pre-School Children's Social Problem Solving Skills
citation: Gur, C. & Kocak, N. (2018). The Effect of TMPT Program on Pre-school Children's Social Problem Solving Skills. Eurasian Journal of Educational Research, 73, 77-94. https://doi.org/10.14689/ejer.2018.73.5
title: Wally Social Problem-Solving Test
description: The Wally Social Problem-Solving Test evaluates young children's social problem-solving skills by presenting images of interpersonal conflicts one by one and asking the child how they would solve each problem. "The test consists of 15 images." Responses are scored positive, negative, or empty, with scores from zero to fifteen. The Turkish adaptation by Kayili and Ari (2015) on 699 preschool children reported a KMO coefficient of .814 and a reliability coefficient of .81 for five-year-olds.
requirements: Administered individually as pre-test and post-test to children aged five and six
constraints: Validated for five and six-year-old Turkish children; in this study reliability was .71 with test-retest of .73
target_learning_goals: social problem-solving skills in interpersonal conflict situations
examples: The test's 11 themes include rejection, making a mistake, unfair treatment, victimization, prohibition, loneliness, cheating, disappointment, having a dilemma, disapproval from adults, and attacks.
key_sources: Gur, C. & Kocak, N. (2018). The Effect of TMPT Program on Pre-school Children's Social Problem Solving Skills. Eurasian Journal of Educational Research, 73, 77-94. https://doi.org/10.14689/ejer.2018.73.5

article_title: The Impact of Concept Mapping on EFL Learners' Critical Thinking Ability
citation: Khodadady, E., & Ghanizadeh, A. (2011). The Impact of Concept Mapping on EFL Learners' Critical Thinking Ability. English Language Teaching, 4(4). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v4n4p49
title: Watson-Glaser Critical Thinking Appraisal (Form A) as the critical thinking measure
description: The study measured critical thinking with the "Watson-Glaser Critical Thinking Appraisal" (CTA) Form A, comprising 80 items in five subtests: Inference, Recognizing Unstated Assumptions, Deduction, Interpretation, and Evaluation of Arguments. It was administered twice, as pretest and posttest, to both groups. The article reports "The internal consistency reliability estimate of the CTA administered as a posttest in this study was 0.81 (Alpha)". Each subtest covers 16 items, e.g. Test 1 items 1-16 through Test 5 items 65-80.
requirements: Administered as both pretest and posttest to compare groups
constraints: Assesses critical thinking via tests only; the authors note subsequent studies should use both qualitative and quantitative methods to examine product and process
target_learning_goals: critical thinking measurement across inference, assumptions, deduction, interpretation, and argument evaluation
examples: Posttest descriptive statistics: experimental mean 54.88 (SD 10.22), control mean 45.11 (SD 5.80)
key_sources: Khodadady, E., & Ghanizadeh, A. (2011). The Impact of Concept Mapping on EFL Learners' Critical Thinking Ability. English Language Teaching, 4(4). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v4n4p49

article_title: Investigating the Washback Effects of Task-Based Instruction on the Iranian EFL Learners' Vocabulary Learning
citation: Alireza Hamzeh. (2016). Investigating the Washback Effects of Task-based Instruction on the Iranian EFL Learners' Vocabulary Learning. English Language Teaching, 9(12). http://dx.doi.org/10.5539/elt.v9n12p16
title: Washback: the influence of testing on learning and teaching
description: Washback is the influence that testing and assessment exert on learning and teaching processes. The article notes the field uses several labels for it and that it can be positive or negative depending on test quality: "The term wash back is itself a neutral one, can be related to 'influence'." The study applies this construct to task-based language assessment, treating quiz type as a washback source whose effects show up in subsequent vocabulary learning. Washback is also said to exist in any type of assessment, including TBLA, where results affect test-takers' future learning.
requirements: Assessment practices whose results feed back into learners' future course of development and learning
constraints: The article notes good tests' positive effects were 'as yet undefined' in the literature it cites
target_learning_goals: Vocabulary learning shaped by assessment practices
examples: The study used task-based assessment as a washback tool and compared its effect on vocabulary development against traditional assessment
key_sources: Alireza Hamzeh. (2016). Investigating the Washback Effects of Task-based Instruction on the Iranian EFL Learners' Vocabulary Learning. English Language Teaching, 9(12). http://dx.doi.org/10.5539/elt.v9n12p16

article_title: Best Management Practice for Understanding Learning in Sustainable Water Resource Management (WRM) for Secondary Science Teachers in Thailand
citation: Chunwadee Chunrasaksakun. (2015). Best management practice for understanding learning in sustainable water resource management (WRM) for secondary science teachers in Thailand. Educational Research and Reviews. https://doi.org/10.5897/ERR2015.2521
title: Walker's Naturalistic Model for curriculum development
description: The article adopted Walker's Naturalistic Model to develop the WRD curriculum framework. The model includes three basic phases termed "platform, deliberation, and design". In this study, a platform was used for describing consensus of concepts, knowledge or learning experiences on WRD, and deliberation identified which concepts or knowledge and learning experiences are needed or essential on WRD. Two rounds of focus groups were used to reach the consensus of deliberation, producing seven essential learning themes that were then used to design the local curriculum framework.
requirements: Requires consensus-building processes such as focus groups with specialists to establish the platform and deliberation phases
constraints: The article applies the model specifically to developing a local curriculum framework on water resource and disaster management for basic education
target_learning_goals: Water resource and disaster management knowledge
Curriculum design competence
examples: Two rounds of focus groups with 12 professional scientists and 9 professional educators produced seven learning themes used to design the local WRD curriculum framework
key_sources: Chunwadee Chunrasaksakun. (2015). Best management practice for understanding learning in sustainable water resource management (WRM) for secondary science teachers in Thailand. Educational Research and Reviews. https://doi.org/10.5897/ERR2015.2521

article_title: An Empirical Analysis of the Relationship between Foreign Language Reading Anxiety and Reading Strategy Training
citation: Seyit Ahmet Çapan & Rumeysa Pektaş. (2013). An Empirical Analysis of the Relationship between Foreign Language Reading Anxiety and Reading Strategy Training. English Language Teaching, 6(12). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v6n12p181
title: Create a warm, learner-friendly FL reading classroom environment and revise high-school reading programs to reduce reading anxiety
description: Based on the finding that strategy training coincided with increased FLRA and on interviewee remarks about instructor style and text difficulty, the authors suggest that "a warm, learner-friendly classroom environment in which the teacher adopts intimate manners may help relieve learners' concerns about reading in an FL". They also recommend modifying reading programs based on learner feedback and revising high-school reading programs to prepare learners for university-level reading.
requirements: Instructors must adopt intimate manners and respond to learner feedback, as the article suggests
constraints: The authors state the sample size was not big enough to yield generalizable results
target_learning_goals: reducing foreign language reading anxiety
coping with academic FL reading demands
examples: The experiment-group curriculum covered activating schemata, skimming, scanning, keeping reading journals and reflective thinking; interviewee Ali reported hesitating to ask the instructor questions about strategies
key_sources: Seyit Ahmet Çapan & Rumeysa Pektaş. (2013). An Empirical Analysis of the Relationship between Foreign Language Reading Anxiety and Reading Strategy Training. English Language Teaching, 6(12). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v6n12p181

article_title: Self-Explanation and Explanatory Feedback in Games: Individual Differences, Gameplay, and Learning
citation: Killingsworth, S. S., Clark, D. B., & Adams, D. M. (2015). Self-Explanation and Explanatory Feedback in Games: Individual Differences, Gameplay, and Learning. International Journal of Education in Mathematics, Science and Technology, 3(3), 162-186. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1075243
title: Warp missions: navigation challenge followed by concrete-to-general selected self-explanation questions
description: Explanation functionality was moved into new "warp missions" where a game character asks the student for help, students first solve a navigation challenge, and in the full self-explanation condition then encounter three explanation questions: "The first question is very concrete and closely tied to the navigation challenge," the second abstracts the solution to a slightly more generalizable form, and the third frames the physics relationship in the most generalizable form. Warp missions randomly select slightly new configurations on replay to encourage focus on underlying concepts rather than memorized solutions.
requirements: Students need to earn a mission score above a certain threshold to unlock levels beyond the warp mission
constraints: The scoring mechanisms were weighted differently across the partial and full self-explanation and explanatory feedback conditions
target_learning_goals: generalizable physics relationships
key_sources: Killingsworth, S. S., Clark, D. B., & Adams, D. M. (2015). Self-Explanation and Explanatory Feedback in Games: Individual Differences, Gameplay, and Learning. International Journal of Education in Mathematics, Science and Technology, 3(3), 162-186. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1066360

article_title: Effects of Blackboard's Discussion Boards, Blogs and Wikis on Effective Integration and Development of Literacy Skills in EFL Students
citation: Alharbi, M. (2015). Effects of Blackboard’s Discussion Boards, Blogs and Wikis on Effective Integration and Development of Literacy Skills in EFL Students. English Language Teaching, 8(6). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v8n6p111
title: Warschauer's text-mediational view of socio-cultural ESL/EFL learning
description: The article cites Warschauer's (1997) 'text-mediational view' as a socio-cultural perspective on ESL/EFL learning that links expression, interaction, reflection, problem-solving, critical thinking, and literacy with various uses of talk, text, inquiry, and collaboration in the classroom. The article states this approach provides a useful framework for understanding collaborative learning in the language classroom and for evaluating the potential of online education to assist that process.
target_learning_goals: literacy development through collaborative online interaction
key_sources: Alharbi, M. (2015). Effects of Blackboard’s Discussion Boards, Blogs and Wikis on Effective Integration and Development of Literacy Skills in EFL Students. English Language Teaching, 8(6). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v8n6p111

article_title: Standardized Patient vs Video Demonstration for Teaching Psychomotor Skills in Spinal Injury Management to Undergraduate Medical Students: Prospective Interventional Comparative Study.
citation: Steenstra Ivan, Flanagan Octavia, Benni Jyoti M, Schreckenbach Teresa, Gayan Mondeep MS, Shrivastava Sandeep MS, Sonowal Kiran MS, Gogoi Amilee MD, Goswami Hrishikesh MS, Pathak Prasenjit MS, Kumar Bhawesh MS. (2026). Standardized Patient vs Video Demonstration for Teaching Psychomotor Skills in Spinal Injury Management to Undergraduate Medical Students: Prospective Interventional Comparative Study. title: Institutionally developed standardized patient program using trained ward attendants for spinal injury skills teaching
description: The authors initiated and developed an SP program at their institute for the first time despite limited resources: "we drafted a scenario-based script for SPs as per the skills to be taught, and we trained our department's 4 ward attendants for 2 weeks and then certified them as SPs for the module." A mock trial run tested performance, honoraria maintained motivation, and the trained SPs were later deployed to train personnel from non-health government departments in emergency trauma care.
requirements: Two weeks of extensive training with a local-language scenario-based script
Peer validation by department faculties and a mock dry run
Honorarium payment to keep SPs motivated
constraints: SP programs place burdens on human resources, finances, and time, and consistent quality depends on SP motivation, training, resources, and support
target_learners: Undergraduate medical students; subsequently non-health government department personnel
target_learning_goals: Emergency trauma care and spinal injury psychomotor skills for first-responder settings
examples: Four ward attendants were trained as spinal injury SPs based on a reference SP program and certified after peer validation.

article_title: Effectiveness of tailored educational content on improving nurses' clinical performance in cardiac surgery wards: a mixed-methods study.
citation: Kazemi-Arpanahi, H. et al. (2025). Effectiveness of tailored educational content on improving nurses’ clinical performance in cardiac surgery wards: a mixed-methods study. Scientific Reports 15, 23616. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-025-08728-2
title: Tailor nurse training to the specific educational needs of the ward rather than relying on general education alone
description: The article recommends that specialized wards deliver training built from a systematic needs assessment of that ward's nurses, because such tailored content was shown to raise clinical performance. It concludes that "in addition to general education, nurses receive specialized training tailored to the specific requirements of their respective wards". The needs-driven methodology is presented as guaranteeing content that is pertinent and directly applicable to clinical practice.
requirements: A systematic needs assessment (literature review, staff interviews, expert Delphi) to identify ward-specific educational topics before designing the course
constraints: Evidence comes from a single geographic region, a relatively small sample, a 6-month follow-up, and a non-RCT design, as the authors state in their limitations
target_learners: practicing nurses in cardiac surgery intensive care units (C-ICUs)
target_learning_goals: ward-specific clinical competencies such as hemodynamic monitoring, mechanical ventilation care, dysrhythmias management, and infection prevention
examples: The study identified 21 topics via literature review, 360 nurse interviews, and a two-round Delphi, then delivered a 72-hour course of 20 in-person theoretical sessions plus hospital-based simulation training
key_sources: Kazemi-Arpanahi, H. et al. (2025). Effectiveness of tailored educational content on improving nurses’ clinical performance in cardiac surgery wards: a mixed-methods study. Scientific Reports 15, 23616. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-025-08728-2

article_title: Does a virtual simulation teaching platform improve surgical training for medical undergraduate students?
citation: Liu Jie, Hu Tingting, Xu Ke, Cheng Zihui, Bu Wenjie, Lin Aiqin. (2025). Does a virtual simulation teaching platform improve surgical training for medical undergraduate students? BMC Surgery. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12893-025-03029-x
title: Self-developed virtual simulation teaching platform for laparoscopic surgical training
description: A web-accessible virtual simulation teaching platform developed by the research team and "accessible at https://www.ilab-x.com/details/page?id=10666&prev=1". It "includes modules pertaining to various surgical procedures, including laparoscopic appendectomy and suturing techniques", uses 3D visualization of anatomical structures, and provides immediate corrective feedback during practice. Experimental students completed 8 additional platform hours covering appendectomy steps, instrument handling, and complication management on top of 12 hours of traditional lectures and video demonstrations.
requirements: Students need instructor-facilitated access to the platform and roughly 8 hours of dedicated practice time on appendectomy, instrument-handling, and complication-management modules
constraints: The platform provides visual and auditory cues but lacks haptic feedback, which the authors link to no improvement in manual dexterity tasks
target_learners: third-year medical undergraduates with no prior surgical training
target_learning_goals: gastrointestinal anatomical knowledge
laparoscopic procedural understanding
surgical instrument handling
examples: Experimental students completed 8 additional platform hours including modules on appendectomy steps, instrument handling, and complication management

article_title: Factors influencing nurses' knowledge and competence in warfarin-drug and nutrient interactions and patient counseling practices.
citation: Subih Maha, Rababa Majdi, Aryan Fatima Sabri, Alnaeem Mohammad, AlRahahleh Mohammad H, Al niarat Tahany Fareed, Saleh Zyad T., Alsulami Ghaida Shujayyi, Almagharbeh Wesam T., Elshatarat Rami A. (2025). Factors influencing nurses’ knowledge and competence in warfarin-drug and nutrient interactions and patient counseling practices. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-07074-1
title: Validated self-administered questionnaire assessing warfarin–drug, warfarin–food, and counseling knowledge
description: A structured, self-administered questionnaire developed from pharmacology and medical-surgical nursing textbooks and validated tools from previous studies, comprising four sections: demographic/work-related information, exposure to health education, knowledge of warfarin–drug interactions (26 items across six drug categories), and warfarin–food interactions (18 items), plus a 15-item patient counseling knowledge subscale. Items use "enhance," "inhibit," "no effect," or "don't know" response options with correct responses coded 1. Content was validated by a panel of four experts (two clinical pharmacists, two nurse educators), and the pilot study (28 nurses) showed Cronbach's Alpha of 0.87 for the interaction subscale and 0.85 for counseling knowledge. The complete questionnaire is included in the manuscript's appendix.
requirements: Administered with standardized briefing protocols and informed consent; scoring classifies knowledge by percentage of correct responses (below 60% failed, above 90% excellent)
constraints: Adapted to the Jordanian and broader Arab healthcare context, which the authors note may limit direct transfer to other settings
target_learners: Registered nurses in governmental, private, and educational hospitals
target_learning_goals: Knowledge of warfarin–drug and warfarin–food interactions and patient counseling practices for anticoagulant therapy
examples: Pilot-tested with 28 eligible nurses from similar healthcare settings before main-study administration

article_title: Video-based e-learning program for schoolteachers to support children of parents with mental illness: a cluster randomized trial.
citation: Kageyama Masako, Matsushita Atsunori, Kobayashi Ayuna, Sakamoto Taku, Endo Yasuhiro, Sakae Setsuko, Koide Keiko, Saita Ryotaro, Kosaka Hiyuka, Iga Satoko, Yokoyama Keiko. (2023). Video-based e-learning program for schoolteachers to support children of parents with mental illness: a cluster randomized trial. BMC Public Health. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12889-023-15426-z
title: WATASHI-KOKO 30-minute video e-learning program for elementary schoolteachers
description: The WATASHI-KOKO ("We are here") PROGRAM is a 30-min video-based e-learning program for elementary schoolteachers supporting children of parents with mental illness. It has three purposes: gaining basic knowledge, recognizing children in need of support, and gaining confidence. Content was co-created with KODOMO-PEER, "the largest self-help group for adult children of parents with mental illness in Japan", based on a childhood needs survey. Feasibility was high: 83 of 86 intervention participants were very or somewhat satisfied.
requirements: Delivered online on an individual basis, viewable during commuting or gap time so teachers need not devote extra hours
constraints: Twenty-six participants judged the length "long"; the authors note a shorter length would have been more desirable
target_learning_goals: Basic knowledge about mental illness and children of parents with mental illness
Recognizing children in need of support
Confidence in supporting such children
examples: Components include gaining attention ("Have you ever met a child like this?"), program goals, parental mental illness and children's lives, recognizing a child, after recognizing the child, a message from an adult child, and self-assessment of learning outcomes

article_title: Ward round competences in surgery and psychiatry - a comparative multidisciplinary interview study.
citation: Vietz E, März E, Lottspeich C, Wölfel T, Fischer MR, Schmidmaier R. (2019). Ward round competences in surgery and psychiatry - a comparative multidisciplinary interview study. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-019-1554-6
title: Include teaching competence and self-reflection on empathy in ward round curricula and the ward round EPA
description: Because teaching was assigned to senior doctors and rarely mentioned spontaneously as part of the ward round process, the article argues educational aspects should be made explicit: "the competence teaching ought to be included in the EPA 'ward round practice'". Similarly, the poor spontaneous description of empathy in surgery is read as an awareness problem, so "self-reflection by using a checklist of ward round competences may help clinicians to increase awareness regarding empathy in ward rounds".
requirements: A checklist of ward round competences for clinician self-reflection
constraints: Further research is needed to determine whether empathy and nonverbal communication are of minor importance in surgery or whether there is a lack of awareness of these competences
target_learning_goals: teaching during ward rounds
empathy awareness in ward rounds
examples: The article cites studies in which first year doctors and trainees described the ward round as a suboptimal opportunity for teaching, and residents did not consider ward rounds an opportunity for teaching
