article_title: Advances in clinical pharmacy education in Germany: a quasi-experimental single-blinded study to evaluate a patient-centred clinical pharmacy course in psychiatry.
citation: Dircks Monika, Mayr Andreas, Freidank Annette, Kornhuber Johannes, Dörje Frank, Friedland Kristina. (2017). Advances in clinical pharmacy education in Germany: a quasi-experimental single-blinded study to evaluate a patient-centred clinical pharmacy course in psychiatry. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-017-1092-z
title: Ward-based clinical pharmacy course combining case-based learning, team-based small groups, and supervised patient contact
description: The course is a patient-centred ward-based placement (2 × 4 hours) on a psychiatric ward, supervised by a teacher practitioner (TP) fully integrated into the ward team, preceded by a 1.5-hour preparation lecture and a 1.5-hour active-learning seminar. Case-based learning is integrated as an active-learning style, and team-based learning in small groups of 3 students is the chosen teaching strategy. Day 1 focuses on taking a medication history and identifying drug-related problems through a supervised patient interview; day 2 focuses on counselling a psychiatric patient, with the TP modelling the counselling while students observe. The course targets final-semester (8th) pharmacy students who have passed a pre-course oral clinical knowledge exam.
requirements: A teacher practitioner fully integrated into the ward team, with 50% of their work time dedicated to teaching activities
A friendly and highly supportive work environment comprising the faculty of Clinical Pharmacy, the Psychiatric Clinic and the Pharmacy Department
Small student groups (teams of 3 students)
Patients asked for their consent to participate
Students with prior knowledge in psychiatric and general pharmacotherapy, verified by a pre-course oral exam
constraints: Ward-based teaching can be performed only in small groups with close supervision, making the course very time-consuming
Pharmacists who work regularly on wards and are competent in teaching are needed as tutors, a requirement currently not met by the majority of German universities
The learning exercises mostly engaged the lower and middle levels of Bloom's revised taxonomy (remembering, understanding and applying), with some higher-level (analysing) learning
The students' total exposure to the clinical setting and direct patient care experience was limited to 8 hours
target_learners: final-year (8th semester) pharmacy students in Germany
target_learning_goals: improving patient and interdisciplinary communication skills
identifying and managing pharmaceutical care issues
counselling patients on drug therapy
taking medication histories
examples: A clinical pharmacy course on an acute psychiatric ward at Erlangen University Hospital, where typical patient illnesses included depression, schizophrenia and bipolar disease
key_sources: Dircks Monika, Mayr Andreas, Freidank Annette, Kornhuber Johannes, Dörje Frank, Friedland Kristina. (2017). Advances in clinical pharmacy education in Germany: a quasi-experimental single-blinded study to evaluate a patient-centred clinical pharmacy course in psychiatry. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-017-1092-z

article_title: Walking Outdoors during Seminars Improved Perceived Seminar Quality and Sense of Well-Being among Participants.
citation: Bälter O., Hedin B., Tobiasson H., Toivanen S. (2018). Walking Outdoors during Seminars Improved Perceived Seminar Quality and Sense of Well-Being among Participants. International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health. https://doi.org/10.3390/ijerph15020303
title: Walking seminar pattern: virtual preparation, small subgroups and student involvement enabling outdoor walking discussion seminars
description: A reusable seminar format in which students prepare by reading and commenting on each other's reflection documents in a social annotation system, then meet outdoors in subgroups of two to four students to discuss while walking, with the teacher circulating between groups and briefly gathering all subgroups two to three times. The article states the form "was made possible by using three previously identified elements for improving seminars: virtual seminars, small groups, and student involvement". A blind vote with veto handles weather, clothing and physical-ability issues.
requirements: A seminar whose goal is discussion and deepened understanding rather than information distribution or note-taking
A nearby outdoor location suited for hearing, since noise pollution would be a serious impediment
Pre-seminar preparation (reflection documents with peer commenting) so students arrive well prepared
constraints: Not all seminars are located next to a park as in the studied case
Four-person subgroups require wide walking paths and strong voices
Staying on topic and seriousness were perceived as slightly deteriorating rather than improved
target_learning_goals: discussion and deepened understanding of seminar themes
reflection on learning and cross-boundary themes
examples: The mandatory Programme Integrating course for the Media Technology and Computer Science programmes at KTH, with four mentor-led seminars per academic year and subgroups of two to four students walking in nearby nature
key_sources: Bälter O., Hedin B., Tobiasson H., Toivanen S. (2018). Walking Outdoors during Seminars Improved Perceived Seminar Quality and Sense of Well-Being among Participants. International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health. https://doi.org/10.3390/ijerph15020303

article_title: Improving rural and remote practitioners' knowledge of the diabetic foot: findings from an educational intervention.
citation: Schoen Deborah E., Gausia Kaniz, Glance David G., Thompson Sandra C. (2016). Improving rural and remote practitioners’ knowledge of the diabetic foot: findings from an educational intervention. Journal of Foot and Ankle Research. https://doi.org/10.1186/s13047-016-0157-2
title: Rural and remote diabetic foot education and training workshop with hands-on risk assessment practice
description: A face-to-face workshop, "2 to 3 h in duration, limited to a maximum of 20 participants, and presented by a podiatrist", moved from pre-test KAP survey through education and hands-on training to practising a foot risk assessment with a risk calculator tool. Post-test, 85 % found the content understandable and 87 % would recommend it to colleagues.
requirements: A podiatrist presenter and small-group face-to-face format (maximum 20 participants)
Supply of assessment equipment and education materials, including 10-g monofilaments and patient education brochures targeted to stratified level of foot risk
constraints: Evaluated only on short-term knowledge, attitudes and intended practice; "the effect on actual practice and foot care processes is unknown"
target_learners: Rural and remote generalist healthcare professionals, including nurses, doctors, Aboriginal Health Workers and allied health staff
target_learning_goals: Diabetic foot assessment and risk stratification according to the 2011 NHMRC Guidelines
Evidence-based foot assessment and eHealth communication skills
examples: "Fifteen workshops were delivered in hospitals, five in Aboriginal Community Controlled Health Organisations", with further workshops across 15 rural and remote towns in the Midwest and Pilbara regions
key_sources: Schoen Deborah E., Gausia Kaniz, Glance David G., Thompson Sandra C. (2016). Improving rural and remote practitioners’ knowledge of the diabetic foot: findings from an educational intervention. Journal of Foot and Ankle Research. https://doi.org/10.1186/s13047-016-0157-2
